rpact

rpact is an R package for planning, simulating, and analyzing confirmatory clinical trials. It supports common tasks such as sample size and power calculations for standard fixed-sample trials, as well as classical group sequential designs with interim analyses. Methods are available for continuous, binary, survival (time-to-event), and count data endpoints.

For innovative trial designs, rpact provides simulation-based evaluation of power and other operating characteristics, multi-stage adaptive hypothesis tests based on the combination testing principle, adaptive sample size or event-number reassessment, multi-arm multi-stage (MAMS) designs, and population enrichment designs. This allows users to start with routine trial planning and use the same package for more advanced adaptive methods when needed.

What rpact can do

rpact covers the main steps of confirmatory trial planning, simulation, and analysis:

Sample size and power planning

  • Standard fixed-sample designs without interim analyses
  • Classical group sequential designs with planned interim analyses
  • Sample size and power calculations for
    • means (continuous endpoints)
    • rates (binary endpoints)
    • survival (time-to-event) endpoints with flexible recruitment and survival-time options
    • count data endpoints

Simulation and adaptive trial design

  • Power and operating-characteristic simulations for means, rates, survival data, and count data
  • Assessment of adaptive sample size or event-number reassessment based on conditional power
  • Multi-stage adaptive hypothesis testing based on the combination testing principle
  • Assessment of treatment selection strategies in multi-arm trials, including multi-arm multi-stage (MAMS) settings for means, rates, and survival endpoints
  • Simulation and analysis methods for population enrichment designs with means, rates, and hazard ratios

Analysis and trial conduct

  • Confirmatory analysis for means and rates in one-arm and two-arm trials, and for survival endpoints in treatment comparisons
  • Multi-arm and population enrichment analysis for means, rates, and survival endpoints
  • Analysis of general estimates and standard errors supplied through getDataset(est = ..., se = ...)
  • Support for fixed-sample designs, classical group sequential designs, and adaptive multi-arm multi-stage (MAMS) designs based on the inverse normal or Fisher combination test
  • Automatic boundary recalculation during a trial using alpha-spending approaches, including under- and over-running

Installation

Install the latest stable release from CRAN:

install.packages("rpact")

Development version

To try features that are not yet available in the CRAN release, install the development version of rpact from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("rpact-com/rpact")

Documentation

Package information and tutorials are available at www.rpact.org. For function arguments, return values, and examples, see the function reference.

Vignettes

Step-by-step examples and tutorials are available in the rpact vignettes at www.rpact.org/vignettes.

Quick start

A simple sample size calculation

This deliberately simple example illustrates a basic sample size calculation with rpact.

Suppose a study compares two treatments for high blood pressure. We expect the new treatment to lower systolic blood pressure by 15 mmHg on average, compared with 10 mmHg under standard treatment—a difference of 5 mmHg. We assume a standard deviation of 12 mmHg in each group. These numbers are illustrative assumptions, not recommendations for a clinical study.

How many participants are needed in two equally sized groups to detect this difference with 80% power?

library(rpact)

getSampleSizeMeans(
    groups = 2, # Two treatment groups
    alternative = 5, # Expected difference: 15 - 10 mmHg
    stDev = 12, # Assumed standard deviation in each group
    alpha = 0.05, # 5% significance level
    beta = 0.20, # 80% power
    sided = 2 # Two-sided test
) |>
    summary()

Sample size calculation for a continuous endpoint

Fixed sample analysis, two-sided significance level 5%, power 80%. The results were calculated for a two-sample t-test, H0: mu(1) - mu(2) = 0, H1: effect = 5, standard deviation = 12.

Stage Fixed
Stage level (two-sided) 0.0500
Efficacy boundary (z-value scale) 1.960
Lower efficacy boundary (t) -3.503
Upper efficacy boundary (t) 3.503
Number of subjects 182.8

Legend:

  • (t): treatment effect scale

This example uses a conventional two-sided test at the 5% significance level, without interim analyses. The calculated total sample size is approximately 183 participants. Rounding up to equally sized groups gives 92 participants per group, before allowing for missing data or dropouts. Power of 80% means an 80% chance of detecting the assumed difference if it truly exists under the planning assumptions.

A more advanced example: adding an interim analysis

We now make the study objective more explicit: we want to demonstrate that the new treatment lowers blood pressure more than the standard treatment. We therefore use a one-sided test at the 2.5% significance level, a common choice for confirmatory superiority trials. The direction of benefit is specified before the study begins. Blood pressure reductions are recorded as positive values, so alternative = 5 represents the expected additional reduction with the new treatment.

We keep the same illustrative assumptions and 80% power, but add one interim analysis, when approximately half of the total statistical information is available. If the evidence is sufficiently strong, the study can stop early for efficacy. Otherwise, it continues to the final analysis.

Simply testing twice at the usual significance level would increase the chance of a false-positive conclusion. A group sequential design accounts for both analyses. Here, we use O’Brien–Fleming boundaries, which require particularly strong evidence to stop early.

getDesignGroupSequential(
    kMax = 2, # One interim and one final analysis
    informationRates = c(0.5, 1), # 50% information at interim, 100% at final
    typeOfDesign = "OF", # O'Brien–Fleming boundaries
    alpha = 0.025, # One-sided 2.5% significance level
    beta = 0.20, # 80% power
    sided = 1 # One-sided test
) |>
    getSampleSizeMeans(
        groups = 2, # Two treatment groups
        alternative = 5, # Additional blood pressure reduction (mmHg)
        stDev = 12 # Assumed standard deviation (mmHg)
    ) |>
    summary()

Sample size calculation for a continuous endpoint

Sequential analysis with a maximum of two looks (group sequential design), one-sided overall significance level 2.5%, power 80%. The results were calculated for a two-sample t-test, H0: mu(1) - mu(2) = 0, H1: effect = 5, standard deviation = 12.

Stage 1 2
Planned information rate 50% 100%
Cumulative alpha spent 0.0026 0.0250
Stage levels (one-sided) 0.0026 0.0240
Efficacy boundary (z-value scale) 2.797 1.977
Efficacy boundary (t) 7.169 3.520
Cumulative power 0.2096 0.8000
Number of subjects 92.1 184.2
Expected number of subjects under H1 164.9
Stopping probability 0.2096
Efficacy stopping probability by stage (under H0) 0.0026
Efficacy stopping probability by stage 0.2096

Legend:

  • (t): treatment effect scale

The output shows the planned cumulative sample sizes and the efficacy boundaries at each analysis. Allowing an early stop usually requires a slightly larger maximum sample size than a corresponding study without interim analyses, but may reduce the number of participants actually needed.

This is an illustration of the workflow; a clinical study requires additional planning, including the timing and conduct of the interim analysis.

Issues and Feature Requests

If you find a bug or would like to suggest an improvement, please use the rpact GitHub issue tracker.

  • 🐞 Report a bug
    Please include a minimal reproducible R example, or a runnable R Markdown (.Rmd) or Quarto (.qmd) document.

  • ✨ Request a feature
    Please describe the use case, affected function(s), and the expected benefit.

Before opening a new issue, please search existing issues to avoid duplicates.

Because GitHub issues are public, please do not include confidential, customer-specific, personal, regulated, or security-sensitive information.

RPACT Cloud

RPACT Cloud is a web-based graphical user interface for rpact. It provides guided, browser-based access to selected rpact functionality, including study design, sample size calculation, simulation, and reporting, without requiring users to write R code.

rpact.cloud

RPACT Connect

RPACT Connect provides access to insights, downloads, and premium support for users and organizations working with RPACT software.

connect.rpact.app

The RPACT User Group

The RPACT User Group brings together users and decision-makers from the pharmaceutical industry and CROs. Members meet regularly to exchange experience, discuss best practices, and provide input that helps shape the open-source development of rpact.

We invite interested users and organizations to join the community, share know-how, and contribute to the future development of statistical tools for clinical trials.

Use in regulated corporate environments

For organizations using rpact in FDA/GxP-regulated environments, RPACT offers support and formal validation documentation for use on validated corporate computer systems. The documentation can be customized and licensed for exclusive use by your company to support applicable regulatory requirements.

The validation documentation also contains the personal access data required to run the full test suite for installation qualification with testPackage().

Contact RPACT to learn more.

About

rpact is free of charge and open source, licensed under LGPL-3. It implements a broad range of methods described in the monograph by Wassmer and Brannath (2025). Formal validation documentation is available to customers and supporting members through the RPACT service level agreement.

RPACT GmbH develops Statistical Tools for Drug Development. We develop and support R packages, Shiny applications, and cloud-based tools for clinical research, with services covering software development, validation, technical support, consulting, and training.

Our products include rpact and RPACT Cloud. We also maintain and support crmPack, the open-source package for dose escalation trial design, simulation, and analysis.

For more information, visit www.rpact.com.
